subtitle: Verified Answer Key (100/100 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Age · Unit I: Drama · Philip Henslowe
items.stem: Who among the following, as the proprietor of the Rose theatre, repaired it in 1592 and in 1595, and spent substantial sums on renovating and expanding his theatre?
items.explanation: Philip Henslowe (c. 1550–1616) was the theatrical entrepreneur and proprietor of the Rose playhouse; his famous Diary meticulously documents the substantial sums he spent on renovating, repairing, and enlarging the Rose in 1592 and 1595.

items.title: Q2 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Age · Unit I: Drama · John Lyly
items.stem: Name the playwright who has written Gallathea ?
items.explanation: Gallathea (performed c. 1585, published 1592) is an Elizabethan pastoral comedy written by the University Wit John Lyly, noted for its mythological setting and its depiction of two cross-dressed heroines falling in love.

items.title: Q3 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Age · Unit IX: Literary Criticism · Stephen Gosson
items.stem: Who among the following had observed in the pamphlet titled ‘Plays Confuted in Five Actions’ (1582), “I may boldly say it, because I have seen it, that ... bawdy comedies in Latin, French, Italian, and Spanish, have been thoroughly ransacked to furnish the playhouses in London.”
items.explanation: In his puritanical treatise Plays Confuted in Five Actions (1582), written in reply to Thomas Lodge's defense of stage plays, Stephen Gosson condemned contemporary London playhouses for ransacking continental bawdy comedies.

items.title: Q4 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary · Unit I: Drama · Alan Sinfield
items.stem: Name the author of Out on Stage: Lesbian and Gay Theatre in the Twentieth Century.
items.explanation: Out on Stage: Lesbian and Gay Theatre in the Twentieth Century (1999) was written by the British cultural materialist critic and queer theorist Alan Sinfield.

items.title: Q5 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist Movement · Unit I: Drama · Jean-Paul Sartre
items.stem: Who is the writer of “The Flies”, an adaptation of the Electra myth?
items.explanation: The Flies (Les Mouches, 1943) is an existentialist drama by Jean-Paul Sartre that adapts the ancient Greek Electra myth and the Oresteia to allegorize human freedom, remorse, and resistance against totalitarian oppression during the Nazi occupation of France.

items.title: Q6 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit I: Drama · M. K. Naik, Shyamala Narayan
items.stem: Which of these do M. K. Naik and Shyamala Narayan claim about Indian English Drama in Indian English Literature: 1980-2000: A Critical Survey?
options: It is the sick man of Indian English literature
It is deeply rooted in the Indian folk tradition
It is essentially a diasporic phenomenon
items.explanation: In Indian English Literature: 1980-2000: A Critical Survey (2001), critics M. K. Naik and Shyamala A. Narayan famously characterize Indian English drama as 'the sick man of Indian English literature' due to the enduring dearth of performable original stage plays.

items.title: Q7 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary · Unit I: Drama · Edward Bond
items.stem: Who, among the following, has written Lear (a play), an adaptation of Shakespeare's King Lear?
items.explanation: Lear (1971) is a radical, political re-imagining of Shakespeare's King Lear by British socialist playwright Edward Bond, examining state-sanctioned violence, brutality, and the tragic cycle of totalitarian power.

items.title: Q8 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit I: Drama · Girish Karnad
items.stem: Who among the following displays an influence of the Yakshagana folk tradition in his plays?
items.explanation: Kannada playwright Girish Karnad drew extensively on indigenous performance genres, particularly the traditional Karnataka folk theatre form Yakshagana with its masks, stylization, and chorus, most prominently in Hayavadana (1971).

items.title: Q9 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Kamala Das
items.stem:
“My man, my sons, forming the axis
while I, wife and mother
insignificant as a fly
climbed the glass panes of their eyes.”

Identify the poem written by Kamala Das from which the above lines have been taken.
items.explanation: These lines are taken from Kamala Das's celebrated confessional poem 'The Old Playhouse' (1973), which articulates the suffocation of a woman's artistic and individual identity within patriarchal domesticity.

items.title: Q10 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Jacobean & Caroline · Unit II: Poetry · Richard Lovelace
items.stem: Who composed Lucasta: Postume Poems, published posthumously?
items.explanation: Cavalier poet Richard Lovelace authored Lucasta (1649); following his death in 1657, his brother Dudley Posthumus Lovelace collected and published Lucasta: Postume Poems in 1659.

items.title: Q11 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary · Unit II: Poetry · Philip Larkin, D. H. Lawrence
items.stem: Which famous English poet, at an early age announcing his admiration for D. H. Lawrence, excitedly wrote to his friend, “I have been reading Sons and Lovers and feel ready to die. If Lawrence had been killed after writing that book he'd still be England's greatest novelist”?
items.explanation: As a young undergraduate at Oxford in 1941, poet Philip Larkin was an impassioned disciple of D. H. Lawrence and wrote this famous enthusiastic tribute about Sons and Lovers in a letter to his school friend Jim Sutton.

items.title: Q12 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Age · Unit II: Poetry · Edmund Spenser, Sir Philip Sidney
items.stem: Spenser's The Shepheardes Calender, published in 1579, was dedicated to ______.
items.explanation: Edmund Spenser dedicated his groundbreaking pastoral collection The Shepheardes Calender (1579) to Sir Philip Sidney under the pseudonym 'Immeritô', hailing him as 'the noble and vertuous Gentleman most worthy of all titles both of learning and chevalrie'.

items.title: Q13 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Augustan / Neoclassical (18th Century) · Unit II: Poetry · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
From which poem are the following lines extracted?

“Some are bewildered in the maze of schools,
And some made coxcombs Nature meant but fools,
In search of wit these lose their common sense
And then turn critics in their own defense”
items.explanation: These heroic couplets appear in Part I (lines 26–29) of Alexander Pope's masterwork An Essay on Criticism (1711), where he cautions against superficial learning and pseudo-critics who turn to criticism out of disappointed wit.

items.title: Q14 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Joanna Baillie
items.stem: Who composed the poem “Address to a Steamvessel”?
items.explanation: Scottish Romantic playwright and poet Joanna Baillie composed 'Address to a Steamvessel' (1821), one of the earliest British literary poems celebrating the engineering marvel, motion, and speed of steam navigation.

items.title: Q15 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist Movement · Unit II: Poetry · D. H. Lawrence
items.stem:
The following lines are from one of the poems of D. H. Lawrence. Identify the poem?

“And so, I missed my chance with one of the lords
Of life.
And I have something to expiate;
A pettiness.”
items.explanation: These concluding lines come from D. H. Lawrence's poem 'Snake' (published in Birds, Beasts and Flowers, 1923), in which the speaker laments throwing a log at a non-venomous Sicilian snake and feels compelled to expiate the pettiness of his human education.

items.title: Q16 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist Movement · Unit I: Drama · Alfred Jarry, William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which of the following plays may be considered as a parody of Shakespeare's Macbeth, and some parts of Hamlet and King Lear?
options: August Strindberg's The Dance of Death
items.explanation: Alfred Jarry's grotesque avant-garde masterpiece Ubu Roi (1896) opens with Mère Ubu inciting Père Ubu to murder King Wenceslas of Poland to seize the crown, parodically mimicking Shakespeare's Macbeth along with scenes mocking Hamlet and King Lear.

items.title: Q17 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Restoration Literature · Unit II: Poetry · John Dryden
items.stem: Who does Achitophel represent in John Dryden's allegorical poem Absalom and Achitophel?
items.explanation: In John Dryden's political verse satire Absalom and Achitophel (1681), the false counselor Achitophel represents Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury, who led the Whig party in attempting to exclude the Catholic Duke of York in favor of Charles II's illegitimate Protestant son, the Duke of Monmouth (Absalom).

items.title: Q18 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Beryl Bainbridge
items.stem: Which of the following is the first novel of Beryl Bainbridge?
items.explanation: A Weekend with Claude (1967) was the first published novel of English novelist Dame Beryl Bainbridge; although Harriet Said... was composed earlier in her youth, publishers rejected it until 1972.

items.title: Q19 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: In a novel of Charles Dickens, a high spirited boy of 19 is left penniless along with his mother and sister Kate, on the death of his father. Which of the following is the novel?
items.explanation: In Charles Dickens's The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby (1838–39), the eponymous 19-year-old hero Nicholas, his mother, and his sister Kate are left totally unprovided for upon their father's sudden death, forcing them to seek assistance from their miserly uncle Ralph Nickleby.

items.title: Q20 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist Movement · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · D. H. Lawrence
items.stem: Penguin Books were prosecuted for obscenity and later acquitted for publishing a novel of D. H. Lawrence that makes a frank description of sex and an uncompromising use of four-letter words. Which of the following is the title of the novel?
items.explanation: In the landmark 1960 trial R v Penguin Books Ltd under the Obscene Publications Act 1959, Penguin Books was successfully defended and acquitted for publishing the full, unexpurgated edition of D. H. Lawrence's Lady Chatterley's Lover.

items.title: Q21 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist Movement · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Saki (H. H. Munro)
items.stem: Who among the following is the author of the collection of stories named Reginald in Russia?
items.explanation: Reginald in Russia and Other Sketches (1910) is a celebrated short-story collection by the British master of social satire and macabre wit, Hector Hugh Munro, who wrote under the pen name 'Saki'.

items.title: Q22 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Herman Melville
items.stem: Who among the following is the author of the novel titled Typee: A Peep at Polynesian Life?
items.explanation: Typee: A Peep at Polynesian Life (1846) is the autobiographically based debut novel of American author Herman Melville, recounting his experiences after deserting a whaling ship and living among the indigenous Taipi people on Nuku Hiva.

items.title: Q23 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Jacobean & Caroline · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Francis Bacon
items.stem: Who was the author of Novum Organum?
items.explanation: Francis Bacon published Novum Organum Scientiarum ('New Instrument of Science') in 1620, proposing a new system of inductive logic to displace the classical Aristotelian syllogistic Organon.

items.title: Q24 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Restoration Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · John Evelyn
items.stem: Who among the following was famous as a diarist?
items.explanation: John Evelyn (1620–1706) is, alongside Samuel Pepys, the most celebrated English diarist of the seventeenth century; his Diary spans several decades, documenting the English Civil War, the execution of Charles I, and the Great Fire of London.

items.title: Q25 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Augustan / Neoclassical (18th Century) · Unit IX: Literary Criticism · Edmund Burke
items.stem: In which year was Edmund Burke's Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and the Beautiful published?
items.explanation: Edmund Burke published his foundational aesthetic treatise A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful in 1757, establishing the psychological distinction between the awe-inspiring terror of the Sublime and the pleasing symmetry of the Beautiful.

items.title: Q26 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas Carlyle, John Ruskin
items.stem: Which among the following was NOT written by Thomas Carlyle?
items.explanation: The Stones of Venice (1851–53) is a three-volume treatise on Venetian architecture and social morality written by John Ruskin, whereas 'Signs of the Times' (1829), Sartor Resartus (1833–34), and The Life of John Sterling (1851) were all written by Thomas Carlyle.

items.title: Q27 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Charles Darwin
items.stem: Who among the following was the author of The Voyage of the Beagle?
items.explanation: The Voyage of the Beagle (originally published in 1839 as Journal and Researches) is the renowned travel and natural history narrative written by English naturalist Charles Darwin following his five-year survey expedition on HMS Beagle.

items.title: Q28 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Augustan / Neoclassical (18th Century) · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Samuel Johnson, John Dryden
items.stem: Who among the following was NOT one of the original members of Johnson's Literary Club?
items.explanation: The Literary Club (known simply as 'The Club') was founded in London in 1764 by Samuel Johnson and Sir Joshua Reynolds, with Oliver Goldsmith, Edmund Burke, and Sir John Hawkins among its original nine members; John Dryden died in 1700, over six decades earlier.

items.title: Q29 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India: History, Evolution & Futures · Thomas Babington Macaulay
items.stem: Which of these did Macaulay's 1835 Minutes on Indian Education want to create?
options: A class of people Eurasian by blood but European by taste
A class of people Indian by blood but English by taste
A class of people Indian by blood but multinational in identity
A class of people European by blood but Oriental by taste
items.explanation: In his influential Minute on Indian Education (1835), Thomas Babington Macaulay explicitly advocated the promotion of European learning in English to form 'a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect'.

items.title: Q30 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India: History, Evolution & Futures · E. F. Oaten
items.stem: Who was the writer of A Sketch of Anglo-Indian Literature?
items.explanation: Edward Farley Oaten (E. F. Oaten) authored A Sketch of Anglo-Indian Literature (1908), which grew out of his Cambridge Le Bas Prize essay and represents the first systematic historical survey of British-Indian colonial writing.

items.title: Q31 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary & Cultural Theory · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Raymond Williams, Stuart Hall, Richard Hoggart
items.stem: Who along with Richard Hoggart and Stuart Hall was one of the founding figures of the school of thought now known as British Cultural Studies?
items.explanation: Welsh cultural critic and academic Raymond Williams—author of Culture and Society (1958) and The Long Revolution (1961)—was, alongside Richard Hoggart and Stuart Hall, a foundational intellectual pioneer of British Cultural Studies.

items.title: Q32 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary & Cultural Theory · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Roland Barthes
items.stem: Who enunciated the idea of myth as depoliticised speech in bourgeois society ?
items.explanation: In his foundational theoretical essay 'Myth Today' (in Mythologies, 1957), French semiotician Roland Barthes defined modern bourgeois myth as 'depoliticized speech' that strips cultural signs of historical contingency and presents them as natural, innocent facts.

items.title: Q33 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary & Cultural Theory · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Raymond Williams, Edward Said
items.stem: Which of the following books is NOT written by Raymond Williams?
items.explanation: Culture and Imperialism (1993) is the seminal postcolonial critique written by Edward Said, whereas Keywords (1976), Culture and Society (1958), and The Country and the City (1973) are seminal books by Raymond Williams.

items.title: Q34 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary & Cultural Theory · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Stuart Hall
items.stem:
Which influential cultural theorist stated the following regarding the formation and development of British cultural studies?

“What is important are the significant breaks - where old lines of thought are disrupted, older constellations displaced, and elements, old and new, are regrouped around a different set of premises and themes.”
items.explanation: Stuart Hall made this seminal observation in his 1980 essay 'Cultural Studies: Two Paradigms', conceptualizing the theoretical trajectory of British Cultural Studies as evolving through radical paradigm shifts and conceptual breaks.

items.title: Q35 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Classical & Antiquity · Unit IX: Literary Criticism · Plato, Aristotle
items.stem: Which among the following was not recognised as a major dialogue of Plato?
items.explanation: Metaphysics is one of the foundational philosophical treatises written by Aristotle, whereas Crito (on justice), Phaedo (on the soul's immortality), and Symposium (on the nature of love) are famous Platonic dialogues.

items.title: Q36 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit IX: Literary Criticism · Aristotle, Giorgio Valla
items.stem: Who among the following translated Aristotle's Poetics in Latin?
items.explanation: Italian humanist Giorgio Valla published the first printed Latin translation of Aristotle's Poetics in Venice in 1498, an intellectual milestone that initiated Renaissance European critical debate on tragedy and mimesis.

items.title: Q37 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit IX: Literary Criticism · Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem: Who among the following acknowledged that poetry is formed from the same elements as prose; the difference lies in the different combination of these elements and the difference of purpose?
items.explanation: In Chapter XIV of Biographia Literaria (1817), Samuel Taylor Coleridge states that poetry is composed of the same elements as prose composition, and that the difference consists in a different combination of them, in consequence of a different object proposed.

items.title: Q38 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary & Cultural Theory · Unit X: Research Methods & Materials in English · MLA
items.stem: What is the standard format for citing a book as per the requirements of the MLA Handbook Eighth Edition?
options: Surname, First name. Title of the Book in italics. Place of Publication: Name of the Publishing House, Year of publication.
Surname, First name in initials (Year of Publication). Title of the Book. Place of Publication, Name of the Publishing House.
Surname, First name. Title of the Book in italics. Name of the Publishing House, Year of publication.
Surname, First name. Title of the Book in italics. Place of Publication: Name of the Publishing House, Year of publication. Print.
items.explanation: The 8th edition of the MLA Handbook (2016) removed city/place of publication and media indicators (such as 'Print'), adopting the streamlined core element format: Author (Surname, First name). Title of Book (in italics). Publisher, Year of publication.

items.title: Q39 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary & Cultural Theory · Unit X: Research Methods & Materials in English · General Research Methodology
items.stem: Which of the following explains the difference between Conceptual Research and Empirical Research?
options: The former of the two is related to some abstract idea(s) or theory, and the latter relies on experience and observation alone.
The former of the two is based on the measurement of quantity or amount, and the latter is concerned with qualitative phenomena.
The former of the two includes surveys and fact-finding enquiries, and the latter uses information already available to make a critical evaluation of the material.
The former aims at finding a solution for an immediate problem, and the latter is concerned mainly with generalizations and formulation of theory.
items.explanation: Conceptual research is focused on abstract theoretical concepts, models, and philosophic ideas, whereas empirical research relies on observable, experimental evidence and verifiable real-world data collection.

items.title: Q40 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary & Cultural Theory · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories & Pedagogy · Noam Chomsky
items.stem: In the context of ‘nature-nurture’ debate in Linguistics, there is a view that there must be an innate core of abstract knowledge about language form, which pre-specifies a framework for all natural human languages and is currently known as ‘Universal Grammar’. Among the following, who is the linguist proposing this view?
items.explanation: American linguist Noam Chomsky formulated the theory of Universal Grammar (UG), arguing that humans possess an innate, genetically determined Language Acquisition Device (LAD) that provides the structural blueprint for acquiring any natural language.

items.title: Q41 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist Movement · Unit I: Drama · Anton Chekhov, William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Which two plays of Anton Chekhov made creative use of Shakespeare’s Hamlet?

A. A Marriage Proposal
B. Three Sisters
C. The Cherry Orchard
D. Uncle Vanya
E. The Seagull

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Anton Chekhov integrates direct quotations and structural echoes from Shakespeare's Hamlet into The Seagull (where Arkadina and her son Konstantin recite lines from the closet scene) and Three Sisters (where Solyony repeatedly cites Hamlet's lines).

items.title: Q42 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Arthur Miller
items.stem:
Which of the following two plays have been written by Arthur Miller?

A. They Too Arise
B. The Real Thing
C. Some Kind of Love Story
D. Tiny Alice
E. The Crying of Lot 49

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Arthur Miller wrote They Too Arise (1936, his first college play) and the one-act drama Some Kind of Love Story (1982). Tom Stoppard wrote The Real Thing, Edward Albee wrote Tiny Alice, and Thomas Pynchon wrote the novel The Crying of Lot 49.

items.title: Q43 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Classical & Antiquity · Unit I: Drama · Aeschylus
items.stem:
Which of these are part of Aeschylus’ Oresteia Trilogy?

A. Agamemnon
B. The Libation Bearers
C. Antigone
D. Oedipus at Colonus
E. Electra

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Aeschylus' fifth-century BCE Oresteia trilogy comprises Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers (Choephoroi), and The Eumenides. Antigone and Oedipus at Colonus were written by Sophocles.

items.title: Q44 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary · Unit I: Drama · Luigi Pirandello, Vijay Tendulkar
items.stem:
Which of these plays feature the rehearsal of a play within the body of the main play?

A. William Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar
B. Luigi Pirandello’s Six Characters in Search of an Author
C. Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman
D. Alfred Jarry’s Ubu Roi
E. Vijay Tendulkar’s Silence! The Court is in Session

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Luigi Pirandello's Six Characters in Search of an Author opens during an acting troupe's rehearsal of another Pirandello play, while Vijay Tendulkar's Silence! The Court is in Session depicts an amateur theatre group staging a mock rehearsal trial that turns devastatingly personal.

items.title: Q45 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist Movement · Unit I: Drama · Bertolt Brecht
items.stem:
Which of these are plays written by Bertolt Brecht?

A. The Caucasian Chalk Circle
B. Galileo
C. Copernicus
D. Archimedes
E. Man Equals Man

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Bertolt Brecht wrote The Caucasian Chalk Circle (1944), Life of Galileo (1938), and Man Equals Man (Mann ist Mann, 1926).

items.title: Q46 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Nissim Ezekiel
items.stem:
Arrange in chronological order the publication of the following anthologies of poetry by Nissim Ezekiel:

A. The Exact Name
B. Latter-Day Psalms
C. Sixty Poems
D. The Unfinished Man
E. A Time to Change

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: B, C, D, A and E
E, C, D, A and B
D, E, C, B and A
A, D, B, E and C
items.explanation: Nissim Ezekiel's poetry collections appeared chronologically as follows: A Time to Change (1952, E), Sixty Poems (1953, C), The Unfinished Man (1960, D), The Exact Name (1965, A), and Latter-Day Psalms (1982, B).

items.title: Q47 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Walt Whitman
items.stem:
Identify the two previous titles of the poem ‘Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking’ as Walt Whitman continued to revise it until it reached the present form in the ‘Sea-Drift’ section of the 1881 edition.

A. ‘Vigil Strange I Kept on the Field One Night’
B. ‘Crossing Brooklyn Ferry’
C. ‘A Child's Reminiscence’
D. ‘The Wound-Dresser’
E. ‘A Word Out of the Sea’

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Walt Whitman first published the poem in the New York Saturday Press in December 1859 under the title 'A Child's Reminiscence' (C); in the 1860 edition of Leaves of Grass it was titled 'A Word Out of the Sea' (E), before being given its definitive title in 1871.

items.title: Q48 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Lowell
items.stem:
Which of the following poems are written by the American poet, Robert Lowell?

A. ‘Anecdote of the Jar’
B. ‘Skunk Hour’
C. ‘Howl’
D. ‘Night Sweat’
E. ‘A Gift Outright’

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Confessional poet Robert Lowell wrote 'Skunk Hour' (from Life Studies, 1959, B) and 'Night Sweat' (from For the Union Dead, 1964, D). Wallace Stevens wrote 'Anecdote of the Jar', Allen Ginsberg wrote 'Howl', and Robert Frost wrote 'The Gift Outright'.

items.title: Q49 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Adrienne Rich, Sylvia Plath
items.stem:
Which poems have NOT been composed by Adrienne Rich?

A. ‘Driving into the Wreck’
B. ‘Transcendental Etude’
C. ‘Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law’
D. ‘The Applicant’
E. ‘Ripples on the Surface’

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: 'The Applicant' is a famous poem by Sylvia Plath (published in Ariel, 1965), and 'Ripples on the Surface' is a poem by A. R. Ammons, while 'Driving into the Wreck', 'Transcendental Etude', and 'Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law' are by Adrienne Rich.

items.title: Q50 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary · Unit II: Poetry · Philip Larkin, Seamus Heaney, W. B. Yeats
items.stem:
Which poetry anthologies have NOT been written by Philip Larkin?

A. The North Ship
B. The Less Deceived
C. The Whitsun Weddings
D. Death of a Naturalist
E. Responsibilities

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Death of a Naturalist (1966) is the debut collection of Irish poet Seamus Heaney, and Responsibilities (1914) was written by W. B. Yeats, whereas The North Ship (1945), The Less Deceived (1955), and The Whitsun Weddings (1964) were authored by Philip Larkin.

items.title: Q51 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Wilkie Collins
items.stem:
Which of the following novels are written by Wilkie Collins?

A. Basil
B. A Tale of a Tub
C. The Woman in White
D. Lapsing
E. A School for Lovers

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Victorian novelist Wilkie Collins wrote the early novel Basil (1852) and the famous sensation novel The Woman in White (1859–60). A Tale of a Tub is by Jonathan Swift, Lapsing is by Jill Paton Walsh, and The School for Lovers is a comedy by William Whitehead.

items.title: Q52 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Thomas Hardy
items.stem:
Arrange the following novels in chronological order of publication:

A. Jude the Obscure
B. Tess of the D'Urbervilles
C. Under the Greenwood Tree
D. A Pair of Blue Eyes
E. Far From the Madding Crowd

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: C, D, E, B and A
D, E, A, C and B
E, A, C, D and B
A, B, C, D and E
items.explanation: Thomas Hardy's novels appeared in the following chronological sequence: Under the Greenwood Tree (1872, C), A Pair of Blue Eyes (1873, D), Far from the Madding Crowd (1874, E), Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891, B), and Jude the Obscure (1895, A).

items.title: Q53 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Thomas Hardy, Virginia Woolf, Charlotte Bronte
items.stem:
Which of the novelists have been correctly matched with their works?

A. Thomas Hardy ~ The Return of the Native
B. Charles Dickens ~ The History of Henry Esmond

(on reflecting that the world is ready to go to war again)

Detestable race, continue to expunge yourself, die out.
Breed faster, crowd, encroach, sing hymns, build bombing airplanes;
Make speeches, unveil statues, make more bombs, hide more bombs
In the mountains, in the caves of the mountains,
The high, deep-buried caves,
Under the rock and ice.

Convert again into putrescent matter drawing flies
The hopeful bodies of the young; exhort,
Pray, pull long faces, be earnest, be all but overcome, be photographed;
Confer, perfect your formulae, commercialize
Bacteria harmful to human tissue.
Put death on the market;
Breed, crowd, encroach, expand, expunge yourself, die out,
Homo called sapiens.

What is the meaning of the word ‘detestable’ in the context of the poem?
items.explanation: In the opening line of Edna St. Vincent Millay's 'Apostrophe to Man' ('Detestable race, continue to expunge yourself, die out'), the word 'detestable' means deserving intense hatred, scorn, and contempt, making it synonymous with 'contemptible'.

items.title: Q96 · June 2023 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary & Cultural Theory · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Michel de Certeau, Michel Foucault
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:

Emergent in the wake of industrialization, studies of everyday life endeavor to bring into visibility and somehow make sense of our humble, taken-for-granted, seemingly unremarkable experience of the quotidian. The project has meant subjecting modern Western individuals to the kind of anthropological scrutiny more often reserved for non-Western peoples. The goal has been to explore patterns of behavior not because they are foreign but because they are so familiar as to fall beneath our notice. Artists as well as social theorists in this tradition set out to register and evaluate the neglected minutiae of our daily lives: the ways we sleep and ambulate, ingest and eliminate, work and recreate, care for ourselves and others, slip in and out of self-awareness, and interact with people, objects, and our surroundings.

Generally speaking, everyday life studies is a science of the "small." Though usually framed in relation to larger social structures, the objects of attention are micro-moments and micro-actions — turning a street corner, stirring a pot, feeding an infant. They are actions that take place without rising to the status of "event." They are moments in time that leave no historical mark (at least as "history" has traditionally been understood). As these examples suggest, such practices are "everyday" not only because they are "ordinary" but also because they typically occur every day, perhaps even every few hours. Whether tied to bodily rhythms or the rigors of wage work, the non-events of everyday life are almost always characterized by patterns of repetition.

Theorists of the everyday, focusing on the effects of modernity, have taken various stances on the political implications of our daily routines. Some have tied their repetitive nature to the mechanization and alienation of labor in a capitalist society. For Michel Foucault, domination is not restricted to the factory floor: the workings of power are more diffuse and insidious than this, operating in the very interstices of our seemingly private lives. For Michel de Certeau, the quotidian is a site not of forcible conformity but of micro-opportunities to defy the dominant order.

‘Everyday life’ as a theory deals with:
options: Events that are mundane and steeped in banality
Events that are part of history's grand narratives
Events that are epochal to the life of a community or nation
items.explanation: As stated in the passage, everyday life studies investigates our humble, taken-for-granted experience and focuses on micro-actions that occur without rising to the status of a grand historical event, dealing with moments that are mundane and steeped in banality.
